from.place: Paragraph 2, displayed derived coefficient-adjunction and inverse-limit calculation, and the following naturality and triangle-identity sentences; foundational enhancement of finite coefficient adjunction diagrams. Technical input: Pinched simplices give a weakly equivalent mapping resolution. Smaller input: Cubical quotient and latching maps of pinched simplices.

title: Cubical quotient and latching maps of pinched simplices
statement:
Use simplicial sets and ordinary nerves of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones] and simplicial categories of [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-lifting], in fixed universes enlarged when needed. Define $\mathfrak C[\Delta^m]$ to have objects $0,\ldots,m$, mapping simplicial set from $i$ to $j$ the nerve of the inclusion poset of subsets of $\{i,\ldots,j\}$ containing both endpoints if $i\leq j$, and the empty simplicial set otherwise. Composition is union. Monotone maps act by images of subsets, and $\mathfrak C[S]=\operatorname{colim}_{\Delta^m\to S}\mathfrak C[\Delta^m]$ in simplicial categories. Let $J^n=(\Delta^n\star\{y\})\amalg_{\Delta^n}\{x\}$, where $\Delta^n\star\{y\}=\Delta^{n+1}$ and the initial face is collapsed to $x$, and let $Q^n=\mathfrak C[J^n](x,y)$. Let $P_n$ be the inclusion poset of nonempty subsets of $[n]$, and $K_n=N(P_n)$. Embed $K_n$ in $(\Delta^1)^{n+1}$ by characteristic functions. For $0\leq i\leq n$, its subcube on which coordinate $i$ is constantly $1$ is $(\Delta^1)^{\{0,\ldots,i-1\}}\times\{1\}\times(\Delta^1)^{\{i+1,\ldots,n\}}$. The simplicial set $Q^n$ is canonically the quotient of $K_n$ by identifying, on each of these subcubes, points having the same coordinates strictly greater than $i$. This description is compatible with monotone maps acting by direct image on nonempty subsets. The nerve map induced by $I\mapsto\max I$ descends to a map $Q^n\to\Delta^n$.

Define $L_nQ$ as the colimit of $Q^k$ over all proper injective monotone maps $[k]\hookrightarrow[n]$, including all commuting triangles among them; $L_0Q=\varnothing$. The induced map $L_nQ\to Q^n$ is degreewise injective. The ordinary geometric realization of $Q^n$ is homeomorphic to the topological $n$-simplex, with these homeomorphisms compatible with injective monotone maps. In particular every $Q^n$ is weakly contractible and $Q^0=\Delta^0$.

source.place: Section 2.2.2, explicit description of Q preceding Remark 2.2.2.6, Remark 2.2.2.6, and the cofibration assertion in Proposition 2.2.2.9; printed pp. 76-77. No Stacks tag states this cubical rigidification calculation.

proof.text: The union and direct-image formulas give simplicial enriched categories and functors: unions are associative, the singleton endpoint is the identity, and image commutes with union. The small colimits needed to define $\mathfrak C$ exist by [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-lifting]. To see that this extension preserves the pinch pushout, fix a simplicial category $A$ and form the simplicial set $F_A$ whose m-simplices are enriched functors $\mathfrak C[\Delta^m]\to A$. By the defining colimit, an enriched functor $\mathfrak C[S]\to A$ is exactly a compatible family of such functors for all simplices of S, hence a simplicial map $S\to F_A$. A map out of a simplicial pushout is a pair of maps agreeing on its overlap; applying this bijection proves the corresponding mapping-out property for $\mathfrak C$. In particular $\mathfrak C[J^n]$ is the pushout of $\mathfrak C[\Delta^{n+1}]$ and the one-object identity category over $\mathfrak C[\Delta^n]$.

source.place: §2.2.2, definition of J^n and Q^n; direct mapping-out proof from the simplex-colimit definition

proof.text: Write $R_n$ for the quotient of $K_n$ by exactly the subcube identifications in the statement, interpreted degree by degree. An r-simplex of $K_n$ is a chain $I_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq I_r$ of nonempty subsets, by the nerve definition in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Put $k=\max I_0$ and $T_a=I_a\cap\{k,\ldots,n\}$. The relation at the constantly present coordinate k identifies this chain with $T_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq T_r$, where $T_0=\{k\}$. This is a unique representative of this form: a generating relation at i has $i\in I_0$, hence $i\leq k$. If $i<k$, the shared coordinates above i determine k and all the $T_a$; if $i=k$, coordinate k is constantly 1 on both chains and the shared coordinates above k determine the same tails. Thus every generating relation preserves k and every $T_a$. Thus two chains define the same r-simplex of $R_n$ if and only if they have the same k and the same tails $T_a$. Faces and degeneracies on $R_n$ are induced by deleting and repeating subsets and, when necessary, applying this truncation again.

source.place: §2.2.2, explicit quotient before Remark 2.2.2.6; agent-written normal-form check

proof.text: Compute the enriched pushout of Step 1 by its mapping-out property. For each $i\leq n$ let $H_i=\mathfrak C[\Delta^{n+1}](i,y)$, with y removed from the subsets: its simplices are chains of subsets of $\{i,\ldots,n\}$ containing i. It is the cube with coordinate i constantly 1 and earlier coordinates 0. An enriched functor out of the pushout is a pair of objects a,b in its target A and maps $\phi_i:H_i\to A(a,b)$. All initial-face mapping simplicial sets have been sent to the identity of a. Compatibility with composition says that for $i<j$, and for a chain in $\mathfrak C[\Delta^{n+1}](i,j)$ followed by one in $H_j$, applying $\phi_i$ to their union equals applying $\phi_j$ to the latter chain. These are precisely the relations that erase the coordinates below j on the face of $H_i$ where j is constantly present: each such chain splits by intersecting its subsets with $\{i,\ldots,j\}$ and $\{j,\ldots,n\}$. The quotient of $\coprod_iH_i$ by these relations is $R_n$: every chain of $K_n$ has the normalized representative in $H_k$ from Step 2, and every chain in $H_i$ reduces by this very composition relation to that same unique normalized representative. Consequently these compatible families are exactly simplicial maps $R_n\to A(a,b)$. The category with objects x,y, identity endomorphisms, empty reverse mapping set, and forward mapping set $R_n$ therefore has the required pushout universal property. Hence $Q^n\cong R_n$, giving the claimed cubical quotient without invoking any coherent-nerve comparison theorem.

source.place: §2.2.2, explicit quotient before Remark 2.2.2.6; expanded enriched-pushout universal-property computation

proof.text: Let f:[n]\to[m] be monotone. In a generating relation at i, both chains contain i in every subset and have the same entries above i. Their image chains contain f(i); an entry strictly above f(i) can only come from an index strictly above i, so the image chains have the same tails above f(i). Thus direct image preserves the relation. These image maps agree with the $\mathfrak C$ maps in Step 1, since on each $H_i$ they are image of subsets, and the $H_i$ generate the pushout. Finally $\max f(I)=f(\max I)$, while a relation at i preserves the largest element of every subset. The nerve of max therefore descends to $Q^n\to\Delta^n$ and commutes with every monotone map.

source.place: §2.2.2, two bullets before Remark 2.2.2.6 and the maximum map preceding Proposition 2.2.2.7

proof.text: For an injection $\alpha:[k]\hookrightarrow[n]$, a normalized r-simplex $(h;T_0,\ldots,T_r)$ of Step 2 goes to the normalized simplex $(\alpha(h);\alpha(T_0),\ldots,\alpha(T_r))$. This is injective. Its image consists exactly of those normal forms with support $T_r$ contained in $\operatorname{im}\alpha$. Hence the images of two faces with vertex sets U,V meet precisely in the face with vertex set $U\cap V$ when this is nonempty, and otherwise are disjoint. Indeed a common simplex has nonempty support contained in that intersection, and its unique preimage there is obtained by restricting its normal form. In a fixed simplicial degree the latching colimit is the disjoint union of the proper-face sets modulo their inclusions. If two representatives have the same image, the common-intersection face just exhibited identifies them in this colimit; it is still proper, since U and V were proper. This proves degreewise injectivity of $L_nQ\to Q^n$. For n=0 the indexing diagram is empty and its map to $Q^0$ is injective.

source.place: Proposition 2.2.2.9, cofibration assertion; agent-written proper-face intersection proof using the quotient normal form

proof.text: First identify $|K_n|$ with $E_n=\{p\in[0,1]^{n+1}:\max_i p_i=1\}$. Send a realized chain with barycentric weights $w_a$ to $p=\sum_aw_a\chi_{I_a}$. This respects the realization relations of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. It is a bijection: for the distinct positive coordinate values $0<v_1<\cdots<v_s=1$ of p, put $A_j=\{i:p_i\geq v_j\}$. The subsets are nested, and $p=\sum_{j=1}^s(v_j-v_{j-1})\chi_{A_j}$, with $v_0=0$; reversing their order gives the increasing chain. Deleting zero barycentric weights and merging repeated subsets shows uniqueness as a point of the realization. The coordinate map is continuous on each realized simplex and hence continuous for the quotient topology. The domain is compact: the finite poset $P_n$ has finitely many strict chains, every chain reduces by merging repeats to one of them, and each corresponding topological simplex is compact by [lem-coef-standard-simplex-compact]. An open cover pulls back to each of these finitely many compact simplices, giving a finite subcover on their union. The target $E_n$ is Hausdorff: distinct points differ in a coordinate and disjoint real intervals in that coordinate separate them. The compact-to-Hausdorff surjection result [lem-sfb-compact-hausdorff-surjection-quotient] makes the continuous bijection a quotient map and thus a homeomorphism. The same argument for the poset of subsets containing a fixed i identifies the realized relation subcube with the full coordinate face $p_i=1$; the nerve map erasing coordinates below i is ordinary coordinate projection under these homeomorphisms.

source.place: Remark 2.2.2.6; explicit finite order-complex triangulation; compact quotient criterion from Stacks Tags 08YD and 0AAU

proof.text: For each $i$, let $B_i\subset K_n$ be the subcube with coordinate $i$ constantly $1$, and put $A_i=(\Delta^1)^{\{i+1,\ldots,n\}}$. The quotient $R_n$ of Step 2 is the coequalizer of the two projections $\coprod_{i=0}^n(B_i\times_{A_i}B_i)\rightrightarrows K_n$: a simplicial map from $K_n$ equalizes these projections precisely when it identifies every generating pair of the defining relation. This is exactly the mapping-out property of $R_n$. In each degree, $B_i\times_{A_i}B_i$ consists of pairs of chains of subsets containing $i$ with identical tails above $i$. Pairing the chains identifies it with $N(D_{n,i})$, where $D_{n,i}$ is the poset of pairs $(U,V)$ containing $i$ and agreeing strictly above $i$, ordered by componentwise inclusion. Deleting or repeating entries commutes with this identification.

source.place: Section 2.2.2, explicit cubical quotient immediately before Remark 2.2.2.6, printed p.76 (PDF p.94); agent expansion of the relation-space comparison implicit in passage to geometric realization. No Stacks tag states this finite cubical triangulation.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-cube-relation-realization] with the current $n$ and $i$. It identifies $|N(D_{n,i})|$ homeomorphically with $T_{n,i}=\{(p,q):p_i=q_i=1,\ p_j=q_j\ (j>i)\}$ in the ordinary product of coordinate cubes. Its projection clause identifies the two realized maps to $|K_n|=E_n$ from Step 6 with $(p,q)\mapsto p$ and $(p,q)\mapsto q$. Thus the entire relation diagram, including its two arrows, is identified in ordinary topology; here $n$ is finite and $i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ as required by that lemma.

source.place: Section 2.2.2, explicit cubical quotient immediately before Remark 2.2.2.6, printed p.76 (PDF p.94); agent expansion of the relation-space comparison implicit in passage to geometric realization. No Stacks tag states this finite cubical triangulation.

proof.text: The coproduct and coequalizer in Step 7 are small: the coproduct has $n+1$ terms and every simplicial degree is a finite set. Apply the small-colimit preservation and ordinary-topological-colimit clauses of [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits]. Together with Steps 3, 6 and 8, they identify $|Q^n|=|R_n|$ with the ordinary topological coequalizer of $\coprod_iT_{n,i}\rightrightarrows E_n$. A continuous map from $E_n$ equalizes these arrows exactly when it is constant on their generated equivalence relation. Therefore $|Q^n|$ has precisely the quotient topology for changing coordinates strictly below $i$ whenever $p_i=1$, leaving every coordinate from $i$ onwards fixed.

source.place: Section 2.2.2, explicit cubical quotient immediately before Remark 2.2.2.6, printed p.76 (PDF p.94); agent expansion of the relation-space comparison implicit in passage to geometric realization. No Stacks tag states this finite cubical triangulation.

proof.text: Every class in this quotient meets $C_n=\{p\in[0,1]^{n+1}:p_0=1\}$. Indeed, $p\in E_n$ has some $p_i=1$; if $i>0$, changing its zeroth coordinate to $1$ is one allowed generating relation at $i$, and if $i=0$ it already lies in $C_n$.

source.place: Section 2.2.2, explicit cubical quotient immediately before Remark 2.2.2.6, printed p.76 (PDF p.94); agent expansion of the relation-space comparison implicit in passage to geometric realization. No Stacks tag states this finite cubical triangulation.

proof.text: On $E_n$ define $t_i=p_i\prod_{j=i+1}^{n}(1-p_j)$, with the empty product equal to 1. These coordinates are nonnegative, and the telescoping identity $\sum_{i=0}^nt_i=1-\prod_{i=0}^n(1-p_i)=1$ puts t in the topological n-simplex. A relation at i leaves every coordinate $t_j$ for $j\geq i$ unchanged and makes all earlier $t_j$ zero, so t descends to the quotient. For the inverse-fiber calculation put $s_i=\sum_{h=0}^it_h$ and let k be the first index with $t_k>0$. Choose $p_i=0$ for $i<k$, $p_k=1$, and $p_i=t_i/s_i$ for $i>k$. Telescoping $1-p_i=s_{i-1}/s_i$ recovers every $t_i$, proving surjectivity. For any p mapping to t, the identity $s_i=\prod_{j>i}(1-p_j)$ shows that p has $p_k=1$ and the same uniquely determined coordinates $p_i=t_i/s_i$ for $i>k$; all earlier coordinates are precisely those forgotten by the relation at k. Thus the fibers of this polynomial map are exactly the equivalence classes, and it induces a bijection $|Q^n|\to|\Delta^n|$.

source.place: Remark 2.2.2.6; agent-written product formula and complete fiber computation

proof.text: The induced bijection in Step 11 is continuous because its composite with $E_n\to|Q^n|$ is the displayed polynomial map. The space $|Q^n|$ is compact: an open cover pulls back along the quotient map from $|K_n|$ to a cover of the compact space of Step 6, and the resulting finite subcover descends since that map is onto. The simplex is Hausdorff by coordinate separation. Apply [lem-sfb-compact-hausdorff-surjection-quotient] to this continuous bijection: its inverse is continuous by the open-set characterization of a quotient map. Therefore it is a homeomorphism. This proves the topology assertion without claiming continuity of the individual division formulas at a zero denominator.

source.place: Remark 2.2.2.6; Stacks Tags 08YD and 0AAU for the compact-to-Hausdorff quotient criterion

proof.text: For an injection $\alpha:[k]\hookrightarrow[n]$, characteristic coordinates send p to $p'_{\alpha(i)}=p_i$ and $p'_j=0$ at omitted indices. In the product formula of Step 11 all factors contributed by omitted indices are therefore 1, and $t'_{\alpha(i)}=t_i$ while the other barycentric coordinates are 0. This is exactly the usual topological face inclusion. Hence the homeomorphisms commute with all injective monotone maps. No compatibility with degeneracies is asserted for these homeomorphisms.

source.place: Remark 2.2.2.6; injective-map compatibility of the explicit product coordinates

proof.text: For n=0 the nonempty-subset poset is a point and its quotient is exactly $Q^0=\Delta^0$. Every topological simplex is path connected by straight segments. For a basepoint b in it and any map of a cube with its boundary sent to b, the homotopy $H(u,v)=(1-v)h(u)+vb$ stays in the simplex and fixes the boundary, so every positive based homotopy class vanishes. The homeomorphisms just proved therefore make $Q^n\to\Delta^0$ a weak homotopy equivalence by the definition in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Together with Step 5 this proves every remaining clause, including both degree-zero assertions.

source.place: Remark 2.2.2.6; explicit affine contraction and n=0 check
